AITech LabHow the talk runs
How the talk runs

A theory tour of agents

Why now

Intelligence as a commodity, the numbers already in production, the trajectory and the economics.

What an agent is

Not a chatbot — a loop: gather context, take action, verify, repeat. Agent = model + harness.

The harness

Memory, skills, tools (MCP), orchestration, context. Designing an agent is software engineering.

From a loop to loops

Don’t prompt agents to write code — build loops that run themselves. Kinds of loops, self-driving products.

Trust: evals

How you know it works: re-running production, LLM-as-judge, the SRE mindset.

The build method

Clarify, draft A-to-Z, evaluate, observe, improve one bottleneck, understand.

AITech LabThe shift underneath everything
The shift underneath everything

Intelligence is now a commodity

Until now

Buying intelligence meant hiring someone. Scarce, slow to recruit, one person at a time. Your output scaled with your headcount.

Today

You buy it like a raw material. On tap, by the unit, as much as you want. A new input for everything your teams produce.

Raw intelligence only talks. An agent is what puts it to work, acting on the world to deliver value with it. That is what this talk is about.

Trajectory

Agents run longer and longer on their own

Length of tasks completed autonomously · 50% success
Source: METR, time-horizon benchmark

In 2023, an agent could hold a task for a few minutes. Today it holds hours of autonomous work.

A clean exponential: the autonomy window doubles roughly every seven months, about 3× faster than Moore's Law, and it has not bent yet. [1][2]

AITech LabThe anatomy
The anatomy · stepped

Agent = LLM + harness

LLM

The reasoning engine. Brilliant, but alone it can only talk. You buy that part; everything else is the harness.

01 Instructions

CLAUDE.md, standing instructions read at every session.

02 Tools

How it touches the world: CLI, APIs, MCP connectors.

03 Memory

What it keeps between sessions, plain files first.

04 Skills

Recipes it knows how to follow, plain markdown.

05 Sandbox

Where its code runs, and how far it can reach.

06 Orchestration

Subagents it briefs, runs and coordinates.

The harness is what turns a model that talks into a system that acts.[1] We walk each part in turn.

AITech LabThe harness · the discipline
The discipline behind the harness · stepped

Designing an agent is software engineering

“Designing agents is software engineering. The primitives are different, but the discipline is the same.”

Angie Jones — Agentic AI Foundation
The agentic code smell
giant prompt · 4 jobs
normalize listing
+ format shortlist
+ calc commute
+ research neighborhood
+ …one more exception

The god-class of agents. It drifts because the script is too long.

↓ decompose, then place each job

reusable process

Normalize a listing → a Skill

fixed output

Shortlist shape → a Schema

exact calc

Commute time → a Script

meaty fuzzy subtask

Neighborhood research → a Sub-agent

The actor rule

Code for determinism · agents for judgment · humans for authority. You do the architecture; the coding agent does the typing — “just let it build it” works, but isn't maintainable.

Source: Angie Jones — “Build Systems, Not Code” (Agentic AI Foundation)
AITech LabThe harness · Memory
Harness · 3/6 · Memory · stepped

Memory, the experience it builds

Memory is just an index — one line per fact, written in plain files the agent edits itself. The index stays in context; the detail is loaded on demand.[1]

memory/MEMORY.md
Memory index — one line per fact
it-stack.mdMicrosoft suite only, never Google Workspace
vp.mdVP invites need an agenda and one decision
muriel.mdReviews every external mail — keep them short
tone.mdHouse voice: plain, direct, no hype

01 Just ask

Tell it what to keep in the moment — it holds that for next time.

02 Write it down

Plain .md files it edits itself — readable, diffable, versionable. One short file per fact, loaded on demand.

Why it matters

A culture of written knowledge is the load-bearing asset. What lives only in a head, the agent can't use; what is written down, it reads, reuses, keeps current.

Sources : [1] anthropic.com
AITech LabThe harness · Skills
Harness · 4/6 · Skills

Skills, recipes your agent follows

A skill is one folder + one SKILL.md — the agent sees name + a one-line description, and loads the steps only when they're relevant.[1]

skills/contract-review/SKILL.md
name: contract-review
description: Review a contract, flag risky clauses, report on one page
— body, loaded on demand —
1. Read the contract, map parties & scopes
2. Walk every clause: IP, liability, insurance, data
3. Flag each risk with the clause it comes from
4. Cross-check company memory for conflicts
5. Write a one-page report, risks first
The skills index — name + one-line description
contract-reviewReview a contract, flag risky clauses, report on one page
superpowersA library of battle-tested working recipes
frontend-designBuild distinctive, production-grade UI
citeAudit a document and source every claim

External skills are instructions you didn't write. Read them before installing — same reflex as external tools.[2]

Sources : [1] agentskills.io · [2] snyk.io
AITech LabThe harness · Tools & MCP
The harness · Tools & MCP

Tools, how an agent touches the world — and MCP

A tool = name + one-line description
get_weatherGet the current weather in a given location
search_webFind pages relevant to a query, return results
read_fileRead a file from disk and return its text
create_ticketOpen a ticket with title, priority, labels

Behind the name, the same shape everywhere: CLI, API, or an MCP server — one standard plug per tool, shared by every agent.[1]

Every external tool or MCP server runs with your agent's permissions. Treat third-party tools as attack surface — install only what you trust.

Without MCP · M × N connectors
With MCP · M + N connectors

An agent can staff other agents: brief specialists in parallel, collect their findings, merge. You stay the one giving the goal.[1]

AITech LabLoops · why now
Loops · why now

Why now — real capability gains

Loops work now because of real capability gains, not hype:

  • Models are better at long tasks — METR: Opus 4.6 completes 50% of 12-hour tasks, ~6× Opus 4. The autonomy window is what loops cash in.
  • Huge tasks already shipped — a Stripe codebase migration in a day (vs ~2 months by hand); Lovable one-shots apps.
  • Loops are built in — Claude Code /loop, automations, the Ralph plugin. You no longer hand-roll the loop.
  • Subagents separate the loop from the work — the loop driver stays small while subagents do the heavy lifting: saves tokens, prevents context degradation.
  • Harnesses are maturing — compaction, skills + MCP, cloud execution. The infrastructure caught up to the idea.
Source: PostHog — "Why we're bullish on loops", Ian Vanagas
AITech LabLoops · the thesis
Loops · the thesis

Don't prompt agents to write code — build loops

The thesis: Don't prompt agents to write code one task at a time. Build LOOPS that prompt themselves — so agents do long-running tasks, and so you can run many of them in parallel.

Two builders converging on the same idea, independently:

Peter Steinberger · OpenClaw

Loops as the way to keep an agent productive over long horizons.

Boris Cherny · Claude Code

Loops built into the harness itself.

The shift: from "write this for me" (one prompt, one task) to "keep working toward this" (a loop that re-prompts itself until the goal is met). This section is the theoretical bridge to the build method.

Source: PostHog — "Why we're bullish on loops", Ian Vanagas
AITech LabLoops · the anatomy
Loops · the anatomy

Engineering a loop — the four ingredients

01 Goal

What the loop is driving toward. "A loop without a goal is a slop cannon." The goal makes self-prompting converge instead of wander.

02 Context

The fuel: tools, skills, analytics, errors, memories. Curated and replenished, not loaded once. For long runs, keep shared state in files (JSON the model won't overwrite), not the context window.

03 Evaluation

The agent checks itself: tests, evals, metrics, LLM-as-judge. Agents verify by using the product, not by reading diffs — and a separate critic beats self-review. That lets the loop run unattended.

04 An Agent

Basic tier: Claude Code in a while true (the "Ralph" pattern), or a /goal command. SOTA: a purpose-built harness — the adversarial planner/generator/evaluator loop (next slide), the thing Ralph never had.

Loop examples — what people actually run
PR babysitter
Watches and shepherds pull requests to green.
Bug fixer
Reproduces, isolates, fixes, verifies — on its own.
Flaky-test hunter
Finds and stabilises non-deterministic tests.
Perf autoresearcher
Karpathy's fixed a 3-year-old bug and found an 11% perf win.
Source: PostHog — "Why we're bullish on loops", Ian Vanagas
Corroborated first-hand by Anthropic — Prabaker & Wilson, "Build Agents That Run for Hours" (the primary actor PostHog describes).
AITech LabLoops · the SOTA loop
Loops · the SOTA loop

Planner · Generator · Evaluator — the loop Anthropic actually runs

PM Planner own context window

One-line spec → a deliberately high-level series of sprints. Vague on purpose: granular plans make errors cascade over a multi-hour run.

IC Generator own context window

Builds. Proposes the contract, then writes code against it — its own context, prompt and job.

QA Evaluator own context window

Grades by using the app — Playwright clicks, screenshots, scores — not by reading diffs. Can throw it all out and restart.

contract.md — what Ralph never had

Before a line of code, generator and evaluator negotiate “done” into a file — scope, tests, edge cases — until both agree (e.g. 27 criteria). The evaluator grades against that, not the planner's one-shot spec.

“Tuning a standalone critic to be harsh is tractable; tuning a builder to be self-critical is not. Self-review is a trap.”

Ash Prabaker — you exploit the gap between an LLM as critic vs. generator.
Source: Anthropic — "Build Agents That Run for Hours" (Prabaker & Wilson)

Self-driving products

The loop engineers already run by hand; a self-driving product runs it continuously.

Not replacement

It is not eliminating engineering.

1% on cruise control

Bugs, UX, paper cuts, conversion — the steady gains, automated.

Frees time

Frees engineers' time for impactful work.

What "self" means here: autonomy from user-instruction as the starting point, not autonomy from the engineer.

AITech LabLoops · the real bottleneck
Loops · the real bottleneck

Code was never the problem

The opposition to loops: it feels like replacement — work abstracted away from writing code. But product engineers already showed code is a small part of the job.

What endures in a loop-driven future is the part that was always the real work:

Direction

Deciding what to build and why.

Taste

Knowing good from good-enough. And taste is gradable — a rubric plus reference examples turns it into a score.

Empathy

Understanding the user the loop serves.

Code was never the problem; abstracting it away just surfaces what mattered all along.

Source: PostHog — "Why we're bullish on loops", Ian Vanagas
AITech LabLoops · synthesis
Loops · synthesis

Loops are real industry progress

Loops are not a couple of tweets — they are an expression of real industry progress: longer autonomy windows, built-in loop tooling, maturing harnesses, subagents.

  • Everything in the harness section feeds a loop: tools, skills, memory, context, orchestration, permissions.
  • This is the foundation for the build method that follows — the method is how you engineer a loop that actually works.

AITech LabEvals · re-running production
Evals · re-running production

Evals = re-running production

Where does the loop's Evaluation ingredient get its data? Not from hand-written tests — from production itself, captured and replayed offline.

1
Capture

Record agent traces in production (or UAT) — real inputs, real users.

2
Diagnose

Find what went wrong — human annotation or automated tooling.

3
Replay offline

Pull those traces into the eval dataset, re-run them as evals.

4
Improve

Scores point the direction; ship the fix — then back to production.

“Don't think about evals as running tests. Think about evals like re-running production.”

Phil Hetzel — Braintrust. This is what lets the loop's Evaluation ingredient run unattended.
Source: Phil Hetzel — Braintrust, "The maturity phases of running evals"
AITech LabEvals · maturity
Evals · maturity

Evals are a continuum, not a checkbox

The matrix you just saw is Phase 1–2 of a longer journey. Evals are not unit tests — start from named failure modes, not exhaustive coverage. As the agent gets more complex, you climb:

Phase 1

Documented vibe-checks

~10 inputs; a human (ideally an SME) gives a thumbs up/down plus a written justification — the justification is the asset you scale later.

Phase 2

Measure to manage

Automate scoring: LLM-judge (subjective) + deterministic code scorers (objective: too many tool calls / tokens).

Phase 3

Whole-trace & tool calls

Score the entire trace, target individual tool / MCP calls; mock external systems, snapshot state for offline CRUD evals.

Phase 4

Advanced

Topic-model production to auto-discover failure modes — no longer hand-named; evals run from the CLI.

← agent complexity growsdirectional, not perfect — trending right is enougheval rigor grows →
Source: Phil Hetzel — Braintrust, "Maturity phases of running evals"
AITech LabEvals · LLM as judge
Evals · LLM as judge

Never trust one vote

  • An LLM judging an output is noisy: ask the same judge twice, it changes its mind.
  • So sample it 3 or 5 times, an odd number, and take the majority vote.
  • A small law of large numbers, for the price of a few extra calls.
  • A small model like Haiku is usually enough: sharpen the question into a simple, unambiguous criterion first.
Always eval the judge

During observability, check the judge’s majority vote against your own labels. Only trust it past ≥ 80% agreement.[1] A judge is not trustworthy by default: “putting a robe and a cloak on an LLM doesn’t make it trustworthy”.[2] Judge outputs are discrete, so the ground-truth set is cheap to build.

Is this briefing properly sourced?
✓
✓
✗
✓
✗
→
✓ yes3 / 5

Five samples, one stable verdict. Use it inside your binary checks whenever a criterion needs judgment.

Sources : [1] hamel.dev · [2] Phil Hetzel, Braintrust
AITech LabEvals · production & SRE
Evals · production & SRE

Production evals: think like an SRE

Benchmarks measure model capability; production measures system behavior — and the gap widens as agents get more autonomous. Past build-time, eval becomes always-on infrastructure.

Eval-signal pyramid — value inverts
bottom

Benchmarks

scalable, repeatable — limited operational value.

middle

Scenario evals

simulate realistic workflows in a sandbox.

top

Production telemetry

highest-value signal — real users, real systems.

The North Star is reliability — with latency, cost and recovery. Accuracy is just an input, not the goal.

Failure-mode hierarchy — hallucination is one floor
topMulti-agent coordination failures
middle
Reasoning · planning · tool execution
foundation
Memory · retrieval · safety

Agent traces = the distributed tracing of autonomous workloads: reasoning paths, tool calls, memory access, state transitions. Logs alone aren't enough.

“Evaluation is becoming the infrastructure — not testing, not QA.”

Source: Nishant Gupta — Meta Superintelligence Labs, “Production Evals for Agentic AI”

AITech LabMethod · Step 1
Step 01 / 06

Clarify the goal

Know what a great result looks like, before a single line is built.

  • Run a deep research on the task: what separates a great output from an average one.
  • Extract the Pareto: the 20% of qualities that make 80% of the value.
  • Turn them into binary checks that sum to a score, your evaluation for the morning.
  • It works best on a task you know how to do well yourself.
Timing

Deep research runs long. Launch it in advance, ours is already in your starter repo.

research/what-makes-a-great-briefing.md
# A great executive press briefing
## Binary checks (score = sum)
[ ] ≥ 3 independent outlets per theme
[ ] Every article less than 7 days old
[ ] Each claim carries its source
[ ] One actionable implication per theme
[ ] Reads in under 3 minutes
AITech LabMethod · Step 2
Step 02 / 06

Get a first draft, A to Z

A rough version that runs end to end beats a perfect fragment.

  • Give Claude Code the research.md from step 1.
  • /brainstorm the workflow into simple skill steps.
  • Aim for a minimal but Pareto-efficient first version: the smallest thing that runs A→Z. Text output only.
  • Wire the tools and data access now, not later.
  • The evaluation layer is non-negotiable: build the binary checks in from this first run.
Secrets & blast radius

No passwords or API keys in the repo. And know what your agent can send or delete before you let it run.

Copy the build prompt
radar — first draftClaude Code
❯ Read @research/what-makes-a-great-briefing.md, then /brainstorm a press-briefing skill
Proposing 4 steps: collect → filter → synthesize → format…
❯ Build it and run it once, A to Z, text output only
Draft briefing generated — 2 themes, 5 sources. Two checks fail: outlet diversity, claim sourcing.
✓ Good. Now we know exactly what to fix.
AITech LabMethod · Step 3
Step 03 / 06

Evaluate on 3 fresh examples

The skill must do the work, not the leftovers of your conversation.

  • /clear or a fresh session before each test. Otherwise the context, not the skill, carries the result, and it “mysteriously” breaks tomorrow.
  • Keep your examples in a folder, you will replay them after every change, forever.
  • Good enough? Move to the visual delivery. Not yet? Next step.

Three test cases cost nothing today and save a paralyzed migration in six months, when a cheaper model shows up.

Copy the test prompt
radar — clean-room testClaude Code
❯ /clear
Context cleared.
❯ Run the press-briefing skill on tests/example-2.md
Briefing generated. Checks: 4 / 5 pass.
tests/
├─ example-1.md · AI in banking
├─ example-2.md · EU tech regulation
└─ example-3.md · competitor moves
AITech LabMethod · Step 4
Step 04 / 06

See inside your agent

Score every example at once. A criterion that fails across the board is the systematic weakness, not bad luck on one run.

  • Ask for a visual dashboard with /frontend-design: criteria down, examples across.
  • Read it by row (systematic gap) and by column (broken example).
  • The average is your single number to move, the red rows tell you where.
  • This matrix scores outputs. Once the agent calls tools, you also score the whole trace — even individual tool / MCP calls. see eval maturity · Phase 3

AITech LabMethod · Step 5
Step 05 / 06

Improve one bottleneck at a time

Several problems will show up. Pick the most pressing one, ignore the rest.

  • Expert on the task? Try your instinct first: the change or new step you suspect.
  • Otherwise, deep-research things to try on that one problem, and hand the list to the agent to iterate autonomously.
  • Validate against your tests. Found a new failure mode? Add it as a test case.
  • Complexity must earn its place: a change that doesn’t move the tests doesn’t stay.
Why the discipline

It feels slow and it is the opposite. Each accepted change is proven, so you never re-debug the same thing twice. The primary debug loop is reading the traces by hand — same muscle as reading a stack trace — not running more experiments.

The inner loop
03Evaluate on fresh examples
04Observe what fails inside
05Improve the one bottleneck
Repeat until the tests pass.
AITech LabMethod · Step 6
Step 06 / 06

Understand what you built

The agent did the typing. Make sure you still own the thinking.

  • Thinking is not understanding. A system you can’t explain is a system you can’t fix or defend.
  • Ask the agent to teach you what is in place: skills like teach-me or make-me-understand quiz you progressively.
  • Have it generate diagrams of the workflow, great to onboard the next person too.
Copy the understanding prompt
radar — understanding passClaude Code
❯ Teach me how the press-briefing skill works, step by step. Quiz me.
Q1: when an article has no named author, what does the pipeline do with it?
❯ It gets dropped at the filter step?
Almost: it is kept but flagged, the sourcing check is what fails it. Want the diagram of the four steps?

AITech LabMeta
MetaCold-start test (Angie Jones): a well-built agent jumps into a fresh context and knows exactly what to do — an AGENTS.md at every level. If "update it to do XYZ" struggles, that's a maintainability signal.

Agents that improve themselves

lessons.md

Referenced from CLAUDE.md, the agent writes down what it learns: every mistake becomes a rule.

Wrap-up skill

A skill that runs at session end: update the lessons, file the test cases, leave the repo clean.

Auto-improve

Hand the agent its own eval scores and let it iterate on its skills against the tests.

Ablation

Regularly try removing complexity. If the tests still pass without it, it never earned its place.

Case study — Anthropic ablates its own harness (Opus 4.5 → 4.6)

When 4.6 shipped, they dropped context-resetting between sessions (anxiety post-trained out), dropped forced sprint decomposition (4.6 holds a 2h continuous build), halved evaluator cadence — and ran at ~half the cost. The rule: “the harness wasn't wrong — it was right for 4.5, the frontier moved.” “The frontier doesn't shrink, it just moves.”

Source: Anthropic — "Build Agents That Run for Hours" (Prabaker & Wilson)
AITech LabThe whole arc
The whole arc

From the loop, to the harness, to the loops

  • One mental model, end to end: an agent is a loop (think → act → observe), wrapped in a harness (instructions, tools, memory, skills, sandbox, orchestration, context, permissions).
  • The frontier is loops that prompt themselves — long-running, parallel, self-evaluating — built on real industry progress, not hype.
  • The method is how you engineer one that converges: clarify → draft → evaluate → observe → improve → understand.

What endures is direction, taste, empathy — code was never the problem.
